title: Virtual reality in the assessment, understanding, and treatment of mental health disorders
abstract: Mental health problems are inseparable from the environment. With virtual reality (VR), computer-generated interactive environments, individuals can repeatedly experience their problematic situations and be taught, via evidence-based psychological treatments, how to overcome difficulties. VR is moving out of specialist laboratories. Our central aim was to describe the potential of VR in mental health, including a consideration of the first 20 years of applications. A systematic review of empirical studies was conducted. In all, 285 studies were identified, with 86 concerning assessment, 45 theory development, and 154 treatment. The main disorders researched were anxiety (n = 192), schizophrenia (n = 44), substance-related disorders (n = 22) and eating disorders (n = 18). There are pioneering early studies, but the methodological quality of studies was generally low. The gaps in meaningful applications to mental health are extensive. The most established finding is that VR exposure-based treatments can reduce anxiety disorders, but there are numerous research and treatment avenues of promise. VR was found to be a much-misused term, often applied to non-interactive and non-immersive technologies. We conclude that VR has the potential to transform the assessment, understanding and treatment of mental health problems. The treatment possibilities will only be realized if - with the user experience at the heart of design - the best immersive VR technology is combined with targeted translational interventions. The capability of VR to simulate reality could greatly increase access to psychological therapies, while treatment outcomes could be enhanced by the technology's ability to create new realities. VR may merit the level of attention given to neuroimaging.

claims.text: A systematic search identified 285 empirical studies evaluating immersive virtual reality applications in adult mental health out of 1096 identified records.
Anxiety disorders constituted the largest body of VR research in mental health, representing 192 of the 285 identified empirical studies.
VR cognitive therapy produced a large controlled effect size of d = 1.3 relative to VR exposure therapy in reducing persecutory delusions in schizophrenia patients.
Experiencing a virtual body ownership illusion of a healthy body mass index reduced body size overestimation in patients with anorexia nervosa for at least 2 hours.

limitations.text: The review restricted literature searches to PubMed, peer-reviewed English-language journal articles, and published empirical data up to the end of 2016.
The paper excluded health psychology, cognitive disorders, personality disorders, childhood-onset disorders, and non-intervention VR gaming applications.
The methodological quality of earlier empirical VR studies in mental health was generally low, characterized by small sample sizes and a lack of randomized controlled trials.
The term virtual reality in existing literature was frequently misapplied to non-interactive and non-immersive technologies, such as desktop computer displays.

future_work.text: Investigating optimal methods for immersing individuals in VR using affordable equipment so that clinical learning effectively transfers to real-world environments.
Testing whether theory-driven psychological interventions beyond exposure can be delivered effectively without a therapist present or via automated avatars.
Evaluating the psychometric reliability and validity of VR-based assessment tools compared with standard clinical retrospective self-reports across understudied disorders like depression.

methodologies.name: Systematic literature review of empirical VR mental health research
methodologies.description: Conducted systematic PubMed database searches up to 2016 for peer-reviewed empirical studies in English focusing on immersive virtual reality applications in assessment, theory, and treatment of adult mental health disorders.
conditions: Immersive VR systems (HMD, CAVE, large projection screen, 3D display)
Focus on adult mental health disorders (anxiety, depression, psychosis, substance use, eating disorders)
